new_statements.quote: As the current investigation of Bayso data shows, disyllabic words have their main stress on the first syllable if the final syllable does not contain heavy syllable –closed syllable or long vowel. [...] However, if the first syllable does not contain a closed syllable (heavy syllable), the stress lays on the second syllable. [...] In case where both the first and the second syllables contain heavy syllable, the first syllable is stressed. In trisyllable words, the stress occurs normally on the penultimate syllable if the word does not contain heavy syllable. If, however, a trisyllable word has a heavy syllable, the stress lays on a heavy syllable wherever it occurs in the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive word stress: heavy syllables (CVV or closed CVC) attract primary stress. In disyllables the default is initial stress (o'.do 'father', ga'l.ba 'skin'), but a light-heavy word stresses the heavy final (am.ba'l 'wind', en.te'r 'husband'); heavy-heavy stresses the first. In trisyllables the default is penultimate (bu.luu'.lo 'ash'), otherwise stress falls on the heavy syllable wherever it is; when the first two syllables are both heavy, the penult wins (gaa.shi.maa'.lo 'water wave', naa.sas.so 'breasts'). Monosyllables trivially stressed. No mention of tone or pitch accent for Bayso.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'primary/main stress' is described.
new_statements.exceptions: kim.bir 'bird' (both syllables closed) stressed on first 'following the general tendency'; derived words (e.g. naa-sas-so 'breasts') said to follow the same pattern; author's examples oo'.ri 'wife', dee'.lel 'girl' stress the heavy first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms of nouns (mono-, di-, trisyllabic and derived words); impressionistic, no acoustic measurement; no phrase-level discussion. Note Hayward 1978 (not accessible here) is the older primary description and may characterise Bayso prosody differently (e.g. as tonal accent, as is common for Omo-Tana languages) - unverified.
new_statements.identity_note: Lemmi 2018 describes Bayso (self-name Giddicho) as spoken on Gidicho Island (Lake Abaya) and at Alge on the western shore; fieldwork mainly at Alge. Same languoid as Glottolog bais1246 / ISO bsw; no dialect split at issue.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.1 'Stress Patterns' (pp. 42-43): disyllables stress the first syllable unless only the second is heavy (closed or long vowel), in which case the heavy second syllable is stressed; if both heavy, first. Trisyllables: penultimate stress if no heavy syllable; otherwise stress goes to the heavy syllable wherever it is; if first and second are both heavy, penult. Summary p. ~57: 'The heavy syllable attracts high stress than the other types of syllables.' No tone described; no secondary stress described.
